variants.name: Type classes with given instances and context parameters (Scala 3)
variants.idiom_name: type-class trait + given instances + extension methods
variants.implementation_notes: Scala's own trait keyword is a mixin/interface, not this pattern; the descriptor idea is the type class: a parameterised trait whose instances are supplied outside the type (trait Ord[T] { def compare(x: T, y: T): Int }), resolved through a context parameter (using, context bounds, summon) with extension methods declared in the type class so operations read like methods on T. The Scala 3 reference says the point directly: type classes add behaviour to a closed data type without sub-typing, and instances can be defined anywhere, unlike an interface mixed into a type's parents; the standard library uses the shape for Ordering, Numeric and ClassTag. Prefer an ordinary trait or abstract class when a single intrinsic ordering is enough - a type can extend Ordered only once, whereas Ordering instances are external and plural, which is exactly the traits tradeoff.
pitfalls: Instance resolution is scope-sensitive: a given that is not imported (and is not in the companion of the type class or of the type) simply does not resolve, while an instance in an inner scope shadows the outer one, so behaviour can change by adding an import.

Ambiguity is an error, not a preference: two equally specific givens at the same scope level produce an 'ambiguous given instances' failure, and Scala 3's specificity rules differ from Scala 2 implicit precedence, so a port between them changes tie-breaks.
Derived evidence is neither free nor cached: a conditional given such as Ord[List[T]] creates a fresh instance per reference, and deep derivation chains slow implicit search and compilation.

variants.name: Type classes with implicit objects (Scala 2.13)
variants.idiom_name: implicit objects/defs + implicit parameter lists (+ implicit classes for syntax)
variants.implementation_notes: Scala 2 expresses the same type class with implicit objects and defs (implicit object IntOrdering extends Ordering[Int]) and implicit parameter lists, often wrapped in the Aux pattern when several instances must be tied to one type parameter; extension methods have no direct counterpart and are simulated with implicit classes, and implicitly[T] takes the place of summon[T]. The Scala 3 migration documentation maps each given onto a combination of implicit objects, classes and methods, so a codebase pinned to 2.13 keeps the descriptor and loses only the syntax.
pitfalls: Implicit resolution follows different priority rules than Scala 3 given search: an instance in the wrong companion object, or one shadowed by a local value, fails to resolve or silently picks a surprising instance without a warning.
Implicit classes used for the extension-method layer add a wrapper allocation and a distinct name in the public API and bytecode, so migrating to Scala 3 changes more than syntax.
Two candidates in implicit scope make a call ambiguous rather than always preferring the more specific one, so implicitly/summon-based debugging becomes part of normal development.
